description:
🌑 ShadowAstra

ShadowAstra is a multidisciplinary team of computer science students passionate about artificial intelligence, space technology, and human-centered software. We aim to build an innovative, scientifically grounded solution using NASA's open data, combining AI, data visualization, and intuitive design to solve a real-world space exploration challenge.
summary: ShadowAstra Atlas is a free web app that finds new places on Earth where teams can rehearse a permanent Moon base or a Mars mission. You pick the target (for example the lunar south pole or Jezero Crater), the job (landing tests, base life, rover drives, ice drilling, lava tubes or a search for life) and your team's limits. Atlas searches all 80,206 land areas of Earth, each about 55 km across and measured with open NASA data, compares every one with the target at the same scale, and returns ten new places: what matches, how strongly, where the analogy breaks down and which field tests to run. A model trained on 38 known analog sites and a terrain AI we trained on Kaggle GPUs help rank and match places. This matters because today's analog sites are few and not well characterized, and a place can look like Mars and still be the wrong test. We tested it in the open: 28 published analog sites the model never saw typically land in the top 18% of all land, and every test, including the ones that failed, is public. Live app: https://shadowastra-atlas.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/ABRUBAB/ShadowAstra_Atlas · Open data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ABRUBAB/shadowastra-atlas
details:
What it does

ShadowAstra Atlas answers one question for a mission team: where on Earth should we rehearse this Moon or Mars mission? NASA's challenge asks for new Earth analogs for permanent Moon base locations and for Mars, characterized with open data and going beyond simply looking alike. Teams already train in a few famous places, such as the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater and Death Valley, but the right place depends on the target and on the job, and no place on Earth copies everything (low gravity, vacuum, radiation).

In the app you build a mission in plain words: a target on the Moon or Mars (for example Shackleton crater at the lunar south pole, or Jezero Crater), a job (landing tests, base life, rover drives, ice drilling, lava tubes or a search for life) and your team's limits. A 3D globe searches every land area live and returns ten new places, away from the famous sites.

How it works

  1. Every land area measured. Our Python pipeline measured all 80,206 land areas of Earth (0.5 degrees, about 55 km) with NASA POWER climate, Terra MODIS ground temperature, plants and snow (via NASA GIBS), SRTM-based terrain, NASA EMIT minerals, volcanoes and impact craters. Each Moon and Mars target is measured the same way from LRO LOLA (118 m) and MGS MOLA (463 m) heights, with LRO Diviner temperatures and ice, LRO LEND neutrons and Mini-RF radar (signs of ice), and Lunar Prospector and Mars Odyssey chemistry and water.
  2. Four challenge factors, weighted by the job. Ground shape (slopes and height range across 50 km), rocks and craters, cold and light, and bare, dry ground. A rover test and an ice search need different places, so the ranking changes with the job.
  3. Two AI models of our own. A learned model (tuned XGBoost, LightGBM and logistic regression, picked from nine models with Optuna on Kaggle) adds what 38 known analog sites have in common. A self-supervised vision transformer (DINO ViT-S/8), trained on two Kaggle T4 GPUs with heights from Earth, the Moon and Mars, compares ground shape and finds Earth twins of any Moon or Mars spot.
  4. Honest results. Each of the ten places shows what matches, how strongly, where the analogy breaks down, field tests to run, the nearest town, a confidence badge, the best 10 km spot inside it (a hint, not a tested result), a printable site report, and links to the same spot in NASA Worldview and Earthdata Search. Every number is labelled Computed, Learned or "Earth can't copy".
  5. It all runs in your browser. The measured planet is about 5 MB of data, so scoring all 80,206 places takes about 16 ms on a laptop, with no server and no sign-in.

How we know it works

With each known analog site and its neighbours within 300 km hidden and the model retrained, the typical known site still lands in the top 2.4% of all land (the learned model alone: top 1.2%). The typical one of 28 published analog sites the model never saw lands in the top 18%. New data only changes the score if it ranks the known sites better; otherwise it is shown as a measured fact (EMIT minerals, Diviner temperatures and ice, LEND neutrons, Mini-RF radar, Lunar Prospector oxides, Mars Odyssey water). Every test, including the ones that failed, is on our How it works page: https://shadowastra-atlas.vercel.app/methods

Also in the app

  • A 3D compare of any place with its target at the same scale, with a movable Sun and a shadow map.
  • A field test on those 3D blocks: a rover or a walking team drives the same route on both worlds, each under its own real Sun, and the run ends with a field log (steepest slope, shadow, climb, drive time, which field tests it supports, where the analogy breaks).
  • Signs of ice at every Moon target from three LRO instruments, read straight from NASA's Planetary Data System: Diviner (cold enough to keep ice?), LEND (fewer neutrons means more hydrogen) and Mini-RF (radar roughness). Six of the seven south-pole targets show a clear LEND dip; the deepest is Cabeus, where NASA's LCROSS found water. Shown as facts, with each instrument's limits.
  • Earth twins: tap any spot on the Moon or Mars to see the Earth places with the most similar ground.
  • A caves and lava tubes layer with 1,062 Mars cave candidates and 278 lunar pits.
  • Three globes with live NASA layers.
  • A classroom page with lessons and a quiz in English, Spanish and Bangla, with Astra, our field-test astronaut.
  • Every score is open on Hugging Face (CC BY 4.0) and all the code is on GitHub.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission teams get a ranked shortlist of new practice sites for their exact target and job, with the gaps written out, instead of reusing the same few famous places. Field scientists get a quick way to check any place against the Moon or Mars with open data. Students anywhere, including in Bangladesh, can see how these choices are made, in their own language.

Next: our scientific validation lead reviews the top new sites; we want planetary scientists to test one of them on the ground; we will add finer slopes from MRO HiRISE; and we plan a classroom pilot in Dhaka.

What makes it creative

Analog sites are usually picked by reputation. Atlas turns the question around: start from the mission, measure the whole planet the same way as the target, and let the job decide what "alike" means. It is honest by design: it says where each analogy breaks down, labels what Earth cannot copy, and publishes the failed tests too. And it brings the Moon and Mars to a classroom in Dhaka, in Bangla.

Factors we considered

  • Scale. Scores are averages over 55 km areas, so the best 10 km spot is only a hint.
  • Honesty. No place on Earth copies low gravity, vacuum or radiation, and the app says so for every place.
  • Validity. The model is tested on sites it never saw, and new data must earn its place in the score.
  • Field ethics. Visits need permits, local partners and care for the land.
  • Access. It runs in any modern browser with no sign-in, switches to a lighter mode on slow computers, has light and dark themes, and teaches in three languages.

Tools and technologies

App: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, three.js with React Three Fiber, Leaflet, GSAP, Lenis and Motion. Data pipeline and models: Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM and Optuna, and PyTorch for the terrain transformer on Kaggle (two T4 GPUs). Quality: Vitest, Playwright and axe tests, with GitHub Actions for CI and uptime checks. Hosting: Vercel for the app and Hugging Face for the open dataset. Video: ffmpeg and our own Python edit pipeline.

How we used SI tools

Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, helped us write and test the code (including Astra, our mascot, who is drawn in code), the data pipeline, the documentation and the video edit. The team set every goal and data choice, checked every number against our tests and reviewed every change. The two models described above are our own machine learning, trained by the team. Our demo video uses NASA footage, screen recordings of our app and the real voice of team member Mohammed Mahmud Parvez. The team card in the demo uses our own photos, cut out from their backgrounds with BiRefNet, an open-source model we ran on our own computer.

Team ShadowAstra, Dhaka, Bangladesh

Abdullah Rubab (team lead), Tanvir Hossin (planetary terrain), Mohammad Saniul Alam (experience design), Tasnuva Arif (development and testing), Md. Tanvir Hasan (scientific validation), Mohammed Mahmud Parvez (film editing).
